content: The metre, symbolized as m, is the fundamental unit of length in the International System of Units (SI). Initially, it was defined as one ten-millionth of the distance between the Earth's poles and the equator. Today, it is defined as the distance light travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second. As the base unit of length in the SI system, all other SI units involving length, such as area or speed, are derived from the metre. Decimal multiples and submultiples of the metre can be formed by adding SI prefixes. The term metre originates from the Greek word metron, meaning a measure, and was adopted into English via the French word mètre. Its first recorded use in English to denote this unit of length dates back to 1797. In the 18th century, two main proposals were considered for defining the standard unit of length. One suggested defining the metre as the length of a pendulum with a half-period of one second. The other proposed defining it as one ten-millionth of the Earth's meridian length along a quadrant, specifically the distance from the equator to the North Pole. In 1791, the French Academy of Sciences selected the meridional definition. To establish a universally accepted standard, precise measurements of the meridian were required. An expedition led by Delambre and Méchain from 1792 to 1799 measured the meridian between Dunkerque and Barcelona, which passes through Paris. This segment was used to calculate the length of the half meridian connecting the North Pole to the equator. However, in 1793, France adopted a provisional metre based on initial results from the expedition. Despite later discovering that the first prototype metre bar was short by 0.2 millimetres due to miscalculations of the Earth's flattening, this length became the standard. Consequently, the Earth's polar circumference is approximately 40 million metres. In the 1870s, international conferences were held to establish new metric standards. The Metre Convention of 1875 created the International Bureau of Weights and Measures (BIPM), located in Sèvres, France. This organization was tasked with preserving the new prototype metre and kilogram standards, distributing national metric prototypes, and maintaining comparisons between metric and non-metric standards. In 1889, the first General Conference on Weights and Measures (CGPM) established the International Prototype Metre as the distance between two lines on a standard bar made of 90% platinum and 10% iridium, measured at 0°C. In 1893, Albert A. Michelson, using an interferometer, measured the standard metre in terms of light wavelengths. By 1925, interferometry was regularly used at the BIPM. The metre was defined as 1,650,763.73 wavelengths of the orange-red emission line of krypton-86 in a vacuum. The original international prototype metre is still preserved at the BIPM under the conditions specified in 1889. To further reduce uncertainty, the 17th CGPM in 1983 redefined the metre as the distance light travels in a vacuum during 1/299,792,458 of a second. This definition effectively fixed the speed of light in a vacuum at precisely 299,792,458 metres per second. Although the metre is now defined in terms of time-of-flight, laboratory realizations of the metre are still achieved by counting the required number of light wavelengths over a given distance. This redefinition also allowed scientists to measure laser wavelengths with one-fifth the previous uncertainty. To enhance reproducibility across laboratories, the iodine-stabilized helium-neon laser was recommended as a standard radiation source for realizing the metre. The current uncertainty in laboratory realizations of the metre is several orders of magnitude greater than that of the second. Key historical milestones include: In 1790, the French National Assembly decided the metre would equal the length of a pendulum with a half-period of one second. In 1791, the French National Assembly adopted the definition of the metre as one ten-millionth of the Earth's meridian length along a quadrant through Paris. In 1795, a provisional metre bar made of brass was constructed. In 1799, the French National Assembly adopted a platinum metre bar as the final standard. In 1889, the first CGPM defined the metre as the distance between two lines on a platinum-iridium bar at the melting point of ice. In 1927, the seventh CGPM refined the definition to specify the distance between the axes of two central lines on the prototype bar under specific conditions. In 1983, the 17th CGPM redefined the metre as the distance light travels in a vacuum during 1/299,792,458 of a second. SI prefixes are commonly used to denote decimal multiples and submultiples of the metre.
